值得閱讀的理由

  • 打破「得民心者得天下」的單一化歷史敘事，從早期美蘇冷戰格局深入剖析國共內戰爆發的國際政治背景。
  • 揭示抗戰勝利後國民政府看似強盛實則財政崩潰、精銳耗竭的脆弱內幕，理解惡性通膨的根本起源。
  • 深入解析東北工業體系與關東軍軍火庫如何改變國共軍力平衡，以及美國武器禁運對國軍造成的致命影響。

摘要

巔峰表象下的虛弱體質

作者指出，1945年蔣介石與國民政府看似站在歷史巔峰，身為聯合國創始會員國並統帥數百萬大軍，卻在短短四年內遭遇全面潰敗。世人常將這場歷史逆轉簡化為「得民心者得天下」，但這種觀點忽略了更關鍵的國內外現實。事實上，國民政府歷經八年抗戰的殘酷消耗，主要稅收重鎮與沿海工業早遭摧毀，財政幾近枯竭，戰後引爆的惡性通貨膨脹實為長期戰爭透支的惡果。表面上坐擁龐大兵力，精銳部隊卻早已在對日作戰中傷亡殆盡，國家基礎在戰後已極度虛弱，且毫無休養生息的機會。

東北戰場：改變實力天平的超級軍火庫

作者強調，這場內戰絕非封閉的內部衝突，而是美蘇冷戰初期的重要棋局，其勝負關鍵並非南京或上海，而是在具備高度工業化與完備鐵路網的東北地區。抗戰勝利時進駐東北的是蘇聯紅軍而非國軍，蘇聯在表面維持外交承認的同時，暗中允許中共部隊在東北發展，並接收了龐大的日本關東軍軍事裝備與工業基礎。這使得原本以游擊戰為主的中共軍隊迅速現代化，演變成擁有重武器與鐵路後勤、足以進行大規模決戰的「東北野戰軍」，直接改變了雙方的實力起跑線。

美援的真實迷思與武器禁運

作者針對外界「美援龐大卻遭浪費」的迷思進行澄清。帳面上美國提供了超過16億美元的租借法案物資，但其中極大比例被計為運輸與後勤服務成本，前線部隊實際拿到的軍火裝備遠低於此數額。更為致命的是，在1946年至1947年內戰最為關鍵的轉折時刻，美國因政治考量對國民政府實施了武器禁運政策。對於高度依賴美式裝備與彈藥補給的國軍而言，後勤補給的無預警中斷成為極其沉重的毀滅性打擊，徹底重挫了國民政府的軍事優勢。

================================================

Many people surely have strong feelings about this question; some believe the KMT was ruined by the United States, while another group would say: >> Don't blame the US. The US gave the KMT so much aid; it was the KMT's own failure. First of all, the US certainly did provide aid to the Nationalist government. During the War of Resistance, the US helped train and equip the National Revolutionary Army, and after the war, it helped transport the troops to the Northeast and North China to take over occupied territories . US statistics show that the total Lend-Lease aid to the Republic of China exceeded $ 1.6 billion. However, this figure is easily misunderstood—it. wasn't $ 1.6 billion in cash, nor was it $ 1.6 billion worth of shells handed to the troops; a significant portion was actually for transport and services , which were listed as aid on the books . Therefore, the value of the weapons, ammunition, and equipment that actually reached the hands of the Nationalist troops was far lower than the $ 1.6 billion stated on paper. However, during the critical years of 1946 to 1947, the US implemented an arms embargo on the Nationalist army due to political issues. For a force highly dependent on American equipment, this. policy of cutting off supplies was a devastating blow. People often ask about the map in the background. This map is not just my dream map of the Republic of China's borders; it is what the Republic of China should look like in the hearts of 1.4 billion Chinese people. We aim to restore the Republic of China, using the Three Principles of the People from the National Revolution to carry out the mission of reclaiming the Republic and rebuilding the nation. We have launched a merchandise bundle featuring a map poster, a map tapestry, a map pillow, and a Republic of China flag keychain. Why choose when you can have it all? Take them all home for just 1911, and now, if you spend over 699 on either platform, you get free shipping. Friends overseas, don't worry. , we will launch international purchasing options soon. Hurry up and grab yours! >> Hello everyone, I'm A-Niu. Today we are going to talk about a question many people learned in history class but find truly incredible when they think about it carefully: Why did the KMT lose mainland China? Chiang Kai-shek in 1945 could be said to have had an incredible start, standing at the very peak of his life. As the leader of a founding member of the UN, commanding millions of American-equipped troops with international legal recognition, his regime seemed impregnable. Yet, in. just four short years, Nanjing, Shanghai, and Guangzhou fell one after another. How did this incredibly lopsided collapse in modern history happen? The central government had millions of regular troops, an air force, a navy, American equipment, and controlled China's most important cities, railways, and administrative bodies, all with US backing. On the other side, the Chinese Communist Party had only just come out of Yan'an, their main bases were in rural areas, and they were no match for the central government in terms of heavy weapons,. air power, or naval strength. Yet, just four years later, in 1949, Nanjing fell , Shanghai fell, Guangzhou fell, the entire mainland collapsed one after another, and the central government finally retreated to Taiwan. It is strange because the central government in 1945 held clear advantages in military, diplomatic, and international standing, yet the reversal over those four years is often oversimplified to " whoever wins the people, wins the world ." But if we examine the internal and external situation at the time, this saying fails to explain why the. Kuomintang held a winning hand only to lose it all so completely. The more you study this period of history, the more you realize that such an answer is far too simplistic. The central government certainly had serious problems: corruption, hyperinflation, low troop morale, land reform, and administrative inefficiency—each one worthy of critical review. So, if we reduce the entire Chinese Civil War to the Chinese Communist Party's main narrative that " the Chinese people chose the Communists ," we are being led by the nose, because many people overlook a massive.

factor when discussing why the KMT lost the war. The Chinese Civil War was never a fair match held behind closed doors between two Chinese parties; it occurred at a time when World War II had just ended and the US and the USSR were beginning a new struggle for the world order. In other words, the Civil War was not just a domestic conflict; it was also a part of the early international landscape of the Cold War . If we don't talk about the US, the Soviet Union, and Manchuria, we probably won't be able to truly understand how the Kuomintang ended up. losing. First, we must realize that although the central government in 1945 was ostensibly a victor, it was not a powerful state with a full treasury and abundant energy. The government was exactly the opposite. Since the start of the full-scale War of Resistance in 1937, the Republic of China had been fighting for eight consecutive years. Major cities like Shanghai, Nanjing, Wuhan, and Guangzhou had fallen one after another, and the most vital coastal industrial and commercial hubs, as well as tax revenue sources, had largely fallen under Japanese control. The fiscal foundation of the central government had already been uprooted. when it retreated to Chongqing. Facing bottomless war expenses, the only remaining option was to recklessly print money. The hyperinflation that erupted in 1946 was, in essence, a post-dated check issued during this long war of attrition. The severe postwar inflation did not suddenly appear in 1946; it was a massive lingering side effect of the eight-year war. The same was true militarily. Although the National Revolutionary Army boasted millions of men, its most elite units had been clashing head-on. with Japan’s best forces since the Battle of Shanghai. After eight years of war, the Republic of China had won the conflict, but it had paid a staggering price in fiscal and military strength. Therefore, while the central government appeared to be at the pinnacle of victory in 1945, the nation's foundation was, in reality, extremely weak. The biggest problem was that there was simply no time to rest and recuperate. Shortly after Japan surrendered, another, much larger war began, and the truly critical battlefield for this war was not in. Nanjing or Shanghai, but in the Northeast. It is hard for people today to imagine, but at the time, the Northeast was one of the most industrialized regions in all of China. During their occupation of Manchuria, the Japanese built massive railway, coal mining, steel, machinery, and military industries there. After the Japanese Kwantung Army surrendered, they left behind not just territory, but vast quantities of weapons, ammunition, military equipment, railways, and industrial foundations. Therefore, the Northeast in 1945 was less a piece of ordinary territory and more of a massive, super-sized arsenal. capable of changing the balance of military power between the Nationalists and the Communists. The question is, who was in the Northeast when Japan surrendered? Not the central government , but the Soviet Red Army. In August 1945, the Soviet Union declared war on Japan and quickly entered Northeast China, defeating the Kwantung Army. This created a very unique situation: while legally the Northeast should have been returned to the Republic of China, and internationally the Chinese central government was the Nationalist government, in reality, the major cities, transport lines, and Japanese. military supplies were under the actual control of the Soviet Army, which gave the CCP a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity. Some might say the Communist Party was entirely propped up by the Soviet Union, but that is too simplistic, because in 1945, Stalin did not initially openly bet on Mao Zedong. Diplomatically, the Soviet Union still formally recognized the Republic of China government and even signed the Treaty of Friendship and Alliance with it. However, as the situation developed , the Soviet Union did provide the CCP with very important conditions,.

including allowing the CCP to operate in parts of the Soviet-controlled areas , acquiring a portion of the Japanese-leftover weapons, and giving the CCP the vital time and space to enter the Northeast and establish bases . The impact of this was immense. During the war of resistance, the Communist army was primarily a guerrilla force lacking heavy weapons. But after reaching the Northeast, the Japanese weapons and ammunition, combined with the Northeast’s own industrial and railway systems, gave the CCP the conditions to gradually transform their original guerrilla. units into a regular army capable of large-scale combat against the Nationalist forces. The Soviet Union did not win the civil war for the CCP; rather, they directly changed the starting line for both sides. What was left behind in the Northeast was not just a few crates of rifles, but a complete war system including heavy weapons, railway networks, and a modern industrial base, which ultimately formed the Northeast Field Army capable of engaging the Nationalist forces in major decisive battles. But even more interesting is what was happening on the other side. While the Soviet Union. was creating this strategic environment in the Northeast, what was the Republic of China’s most important ally, the United States, doing? This is a question many people will surely argue about; some believe that >> the Nationalist Party was doomed by the United States, >> while another group will say >> Forget the US; the US gave the KMT so much aid, the KMT was just too incompetent itself. Actually, both sides are only half right. First of all , of course the US provided aid to the Nationalist government. During the War of Resistance, the US helped train and equip the Nationalist army, and after the war, it helped transport them to. the Northeast and North China to receive surrendered territories. The US recorded total Lend-Lease aid to the Republic of China at over 1.6 billion dollars, but this figure easily causes misunderstandings; it was not 1.6 billion in cash, nor did it all go toward artillery shells for the Nationalist army. A significant portion actually consisted of transportation and services, such as helping to move Nationalist troops to North China and the Northeast, which are included in the aid balance sheet, so the actual value of weapons, ammunition, and equipment directly in the hands of the. army was far lower than the 1.6 billion dollar figure. Furthermore, compared to US investment in other major allies, the aid received by the Republic of China was surprisingly low; the Soviet Union received several times more, to say nothing of the scale provided to Britain. Therefore, the claim that "the US armed the KMT to the teeth, only for them to hand all their gear to the Communists" tends to overestimate the actual scale of the aid and the portion that could be directly used in the Chinese Civil War. But that is not the. most important issue; the most important thing is that US aid to the Nationalist government did not mean the US was willing to help destroy the Communists. With World War II just over , the last thing the US wanted to see was an immediate, large-scale civil war in China involving millions. It was a total civil war, which is why Truman sent Marshall to China to mediate. The US hoped for a ceasefire, negotiations, and KMT-CCP cooperation, but Chiang Kai-shek believed the CCP was expanding rapidly and would only be harder to deal with later, so the Republic of. China and the US fundamentally lacked shared strategic goals on whether to fight this war to the end. This leads to a highly controversial issue, often rumored as "the US provided guns but no bullets," but the truth lies in a more complex logistical breakdown. The Nationalist army began re-equipping with US gear at the end of the war, but during the critical years of 1946 to 1947, the US imposed an arms embargo on the Nationalist army due to political issues; for a force highly dependent on.

American equipment, this policy was a lethal blow. Even US government documents acknowledged that the deterioration of the Nationalist army's situation at the time, besides issues with high-level command and morale, was also significantly hampered by a shortage of ammunition. So a more accurate statement is that it wasn't that the US never provided bullets, but rather that after the Nationalist army partially Americanized, it faced political restrictions on arms procurement from the US at a crucial stage of the civil war, and this impact cannot be ignored. But we cannot blame. America entirely, as the Nationalist Army's own ammunition management and logistics systems had serious flaws. Caught in the cracks on the eve of the US-Soviet Cold War, the central government faced a very awkward diplomatic situation. America, ostensibly an ally, had a strategic bottom line of avoiding entanglement in a full-scale Asian war and thus worked hard to contain the civil war, while the Soviet Union, which recognized the Republic of China by treaty, secretly ceded space and supplies in the Northeast to bolster the CCP. When the. strategic goals of an ally diverge from one's own survival interests, foreign aid can actually become a political shackle, which is why the central government faced such a difficult international environment. America was not an enemy, but rather our most important ally; however, the outcome the U.S. desired was not the outcome Chiang Kai-shek wanted. This is why I do not believe 1949 can be explained solely by the Nationalist Party losing popular support. The CCP’s primary narrative regarding the Civil War is that "the Nationalist Party lost the. people's hearts, so the Communists won the world." In an era without universal suffrage, military victory and democratic mandate cannot be equated. What the CCP demonstrated was not democratic consensus based on votes, but precise interest-based exchanges and organizational mobilization. For impoverished tenant farmers, the abstract "Five-Power Constitution" could not compare to the immediate prospect of land redistribution. The Communist Party's organizational ability in rural areas was indeed far superior to the Nationalists. Rent reduction, land reform, peasant associations, militias, party branches,. and political propaganda—the CCP wove all these elements together. For many poor farmers, land was the most direct benefit. If you go to someone today who has no fields and cannot get enough to eat...If you talk to a starving farmer about freedom, democracy, or the constitution, he might not understand; but if the Communist Party tells him, " Follow me, and the landlord's land will be given to you," he certainly understands that. Of course, the CCP's subsequent land reform was accompanied by cruel class struggle, violence, and killing. We cannot romanticize it, but from the perspective of war. mobilization alone, it was highly effective. The CCP integrated peasants, food, intelligence, recruitment, and transport entirely into their party structure. So the situation was more like the Nationalists had the state, while the Communists had better organization. However, having the ability to mobilize the masses does not equate to receiving a democratic mandate from all Chinese people. Therefore, a more accurate statement is that the Nationalists lost the world, not that the Communists won the people's hearts. The outcome of war is inherently the result of a combination. of military, organizational, financial, diplomatic, and international factors. If we blame the Nationalist failure entirely on the U.S. and the Soviet Union, we are simply moving from one form of historical reductionism to another. The Nationalist government faced its own severe problems, the first and most fatal being hyperinflation. The Nationalist government had been printing money in massive quantities since the War of Resistance, and the astronomical military spending after the civil war broke out caused the fiscal situation to collapse. In 1947 alone, the.

issuance of legal tender increased more than eightfold, while rice prices in Shanghai surged over 15 times, with the majority of government spending diverted to the military. By 1948, the situation was completely out of control . The Nationalist government introduced the Gold Yuan, hoping to solve the inflation issue in one stroke, and even demanded that the people exchange their gold, silver, and foreign currency for these notes. Soon after its launch, the Gold Yuan plummeted in value, leading to dire consequences because who relied on currency the most? Civil servants, teachers, soldiers, the middle class,. and business owners in the cities. Farmers at least had land and food, but for a professor in Shanghai or a civil servant in Nanjing, their salaries would become worthless scraps of paper within days of receipt. How could they not lose faith in the government? So it seemed that before the Communists even entered Shanghai, the Nationalist government had already destroyed its own urban base through hyperinflation. The second issue was government credibility, but it must be clarified that in 1945, at the time of victory in the war, the central government was not. without prestige. On the contrary, Chiang Kai-shek and the Nationalist government were at the peak of their popularity. After eight years of war, the Republic of China had finally become a victor. Many people in the occupied territories truly longed for the central government to return, and the Nationalist troops were welcomed by crowds when they entered cities like Shanghai and Nanjing. Therefore, the problem in 1945 was not that the people didn't trust the Nationalist government , but rather that their expectations for it were too high. Everyone thought that with the war finally over, what. would follow was peaceful reconstruction, economic recovery, and constitutional development; however, the reality of the ensuing years was a massive disappointment. The post-war takeover was marred by widespread chaos and corruption, even being mocked by the public as "taking over the spoils." As the fighting expanded, from the conscription of troops and grain to the total collapse of fiscal policy, the public's optimistic expectations for the new regime rapidly turned into a severe collapse of confidence within just two or three years. The political credibility of the Nationalist. government did not vanish suddenly in 1945; instead, it was rapidly depleted from a very high position between 1946 and 1948. By the later stages of the Chinese Civil War, what the central government had truly lost was less about abstract prestige and more about the shift from the public's high expectations in 1945 to their deep disappointment in the government's ability to govern. The third issue is the military; many people would say the Nationalist army was just too incompetent and was crushed by the Communist forces. But this explanation is far too simplistic. The Nationalist army was not entirely incapable of. fighting; the War of Resistance and the Burma Campaign both proved that certain Nationalist units possessed significant combat effectiveness. The real problem was that the Nationalist army was never a highly integrated and assimilated modern national force. It consisted of central troops, local provincial forces , former warlord units, absorbed troops , and even reorganized puppet forces after the war, with massive disparities in loyalty, training, equipment, and combat morale among them. Furthermore, Chiang Kai-shek’s high level of intervention in military command and his lack of trust in his generals,. combined with internal factionalism, created issues. Once the economy began to collapse, military purchasing power plummeted, logistics failed, and with a large influx of forced conscripts, the entire force began to lose its resilience. Therefore, the Kuomintang’s loss of the mainland cannot be attributed solely to Chiang Kai-shek’s inability to lead troops in battle. As the supreme leader, Chiang naturally bears the ultimate political responsibility for the failure, but the total collapse of an army of millions and a nation of hundreds of millions within a few years.

could not have been caused by one person’s military ability alone. By 1948, all the problems the Kuomintang had accumulated began to explode at once, starting with the Liaoshen Campaign, which is why we spent so much time discussing the Northeast earlier. Once the Northeast was lost, the central government didn’t just lose a vast territory and a large number of elite frontline troops; more importantly, the CCP gained real control over major industrial hubs and military bases. Next was the Xuzhou-Bengbu Campaign, which even more clearly highlighted the gap in. organizational capabilities between the Kuomintang and the Communists. The CCP was able to mobilize a massive number of peasants to assist in transporting food, ammunition, and the wounded. This doesn’t mean every peasant pushing a cart was a devout communist; it truly demonstrates that the Party’s organization had penetrated the grassroots, turning the vast resources of a rural society into war-fighting capability. After the Pingjin Campaign ended and the situation in North China was settled, the Kuomintang suffered a total collapse at this point. My view. is that it wasn't the loss of the three major campaigns that caused the sudden loss of China; rather, the Nationalist government’s finances, political credibility, military morale, grassroots organization, and international standing had all faced severe problems simultaneously, and the three campaigns simply brought all these issues to a head. We can finally answer today's question: why did the Kuomintang lose the entire mainland? It was not due to a single reason, nor can it be explained by the simple phrase of "losing the hearts and minds of the. people." On the surface, the Kuomintang possessed everything a modern state should have: a central government, an army, diplomatic recognition, a central bank, administrative agencies, and international allies. However, a truly effective modern state requires more than just flying a flag or setting up ministries. You must be able to stabilize the currency, collect taxes, govern regions, maintain effective logistics, nationalize the military, promote social reform, gain the people's trust, and at the same time, secure a favorable strategic environment in international politics. By 1948-49, the central government was steadily losing these capabilities, which is why I would argue that what the Kuomintang truly lost was its state capacity. The Nationalist government's own governance crisis, combined with the CCP's stronger grassroots organizational ability and the post-WWII shift in U.S. policy toward China, together determined the outcome of the civil war. However, this leads to a very interesting question: if the KMT truly lacked any governance ability , had completely lost popular support, and was destined to be discarded by. history, why didn't it lose again after retreating to Taiwan, but instead managed to slowly stabilize? I believe this is exactly the most thought-provoking aspect of analyzing this history. After the central government withdrew to Taiwan, it accomplished many things it had failed or lacked the capacity to do on the mainland: restructuring finances, stabilizing the currency, reorganizing the military, improving the administrative system, and most importantly, land reform—starting with the 375 Rent Reduction in 1949, followed by the sale of public land, and leading to the "Land to the Tiller" program in 1953, which turned many. tenant farmers into landowners. Has everyone noticed a rather ironic fact? The land issue was never the exclusive domain of the Communist Party. The Founding Father, Sun Yat-sen, had already proposed the "equalization of land rights" in the Three Principles of the People; the National Revolution understood from the beginning that if a country's land and wealth are highly concentrated and the vast majority of farmers lack basic economic security, it is very difficult to achieve true political and social stability. The problem was that while on the mainland, the central government was constrained by wars, warlords, local factions, and.

the existing social structure, making it impossible to fully implement the equalization of land rights. The Communist Party, instead, used more radical—even violent and class-struggle-driven—methods to seize this key political issue that originally belonged to the Three Principles of the People. After reaching Taiwan, the KMT finally had the opportunity, within a smaller territory where government control was more intact, to truly carry out land reform. Therefore, I believe the fact that the KMT was able to gain a firm footing in Taiwan proves that its failure on the mainland did not. represent a failure of the Three Principles of the People itself; rather , it was because the central government of that time simply did not have enough time to complete the National Revolution. Thus, 1949 cannot be simply described as the Chinese people abandoning the KMT for the CCP, because the Chinese people never made such a choice in a free election. What truly happened in 1949 was that the Republic of China, having just endured eight years of war, with a near-collapsed economy and an exhausted society, was immediately plunged into another full-scale civil war. It faced a CCP. that had secured strategic conditions in Manchuria and possessed immense grassroots organizational power, while simultaneously dealing with a United States that preferred mediation and was unwilling to support the destruction of the CCP, as well as a Soviet Union that nominally recognized the Republic of China but provided the CCP with critical conditions for growth—all this, combined with the government's own hyperinflation, corruption, insufficient land reform, and issues with its military and administrative systems, resulted in the events of 1949 . Therefore, I believe the collapse of the KMT in 1949 was not simply a military defeat on paper, but the. result of the state's fiscal, organizational, diplomatic, and military systems unraveling after eight years of war, before a modern national framework had even been established. But in the end, I want to return to what this channel has always cared about most: the KMT losing the mainland in 1949 does not mean the National Revolution failed, because its goal was never to keep the KMT in power forever. Dr. Sun Yat-sen pursued the Three Principles of the People—nationalism,. democracy, and the people's livelihood —to build a democratic republic that truly belongs to the citizens, where the people can choose their government, the military belongs to the state rather than a party or leader, and the people enjoy freedom and basic rights, ensuring economic growth benefits more than just a select few. Regrettably, by 1949, these goals had not yet been fully achieved. While the CCP won the civil war militarily, they did not complete China's democratic revolution; instead, they established a. totalitarian regime under one-party rule. So, our discussion today on why the KMT lost mainland China is not meant to vindicate them. Our true purpose is to look back at this massive historical failure to better understand what a truly modernized China actually requires. What it needs is not an infallible great leader, but democratic constitutionalism, a nationalized military, an effective and accountable government, localized governance, and a. system for the people to share in the fruits of development—all of which the National Revolution began seeking over a century ago. It is just that this path has been incredibly long and filled with failures, to the point where we nearly lost all of China in 1949. However, 1949 was not the end of China's pursuit of a democratic republic. The Republic of China’s eventual transition to democracy in Taiwan proves that Chinese people are not incapable of democracy, nor are they destined to accept one-party rule.

When the day finally comes that the Chinese people on the mainland can freely elect their government, criticize their leaders, form parties, publish freely, practice their faith, and see their military nationalized and their constitution truly protect them, we can look back at 1949 not as just the KMT's defeat, but as a massive, painful setback on China's long journey toward becoming a republic. The spirit of the National Revolution may suffer a. hundred setbacks, but it will never end . Alright, that is all for today’s story. If you enjoyed this episode, please subscribe and share it. 值得閱讀的理由

  • 打破「得民心者得天下」的單一化歷史敘事，從早期美蘇冷戰格局深入剖析國共內戰爆發的國際政治背景。

  • 深入解析東北工業體系與關東軍軍火庫如何改變國共軍力平衡，以及美國武器禁運對國軍造成的致命影響。

摘要

巔峰表象下的虛弱體質

值得閱讀的理由

  • 打破「得民心者得天下」的單一化歷史敘事，從早期美蘇冷戰格局深入剖析國共內戰爆發的國際政治背景。
  • 揭示抗戰勝利後國民政府看似強盛實則財政崩潰、精銳耗竭的脆弱內幕，理解惡性通膨的根本起源。
  • 深入解析東北工業體系與關東軍軍火庫如何改變國共軍力平衡，以及美國武器禁運對國軍造成的致命影響。

摘要

巔峰表象下的虛弱體質

作者指出，1945年蔣介石與國民政府看似站在歷史巔峰，身為聯合國創始會員國並統帥數百萬大軍，卻在短短四年內遭遇全面潰敗。世人常將這場歷史逆轉簡化為「得民心者得天下」，但這種觀點忽略了更關鍵的國內外現實。事實上，國民政府歷經八年抗戰的殘酷消耗，主要稅收重鎮與沿海工業早遭摧毀，財政幾近枯竭，戰後引爆的惡性通貨膨脹實為長期戰爭透支的惡果。表面上坐擁龐大兵力，精銳部隊卻早已在對日作戰中傷亡殆盡，國家基礎在戰後已極度虛弱，且毫無休養生息的機會。

東北戰場：改變實力天平的超級軍火庫

作者強調，這場內戰絕非封閉的內部衝突，而是美蘇冷戰初期的重要棋局，其勝負關鍵並非南京或上海，而是在具備高度工業化與完備鐵路網的東北地區。抗戰勝利時進駐東北的是蘇聯紅軍而非國軍，蘇聯在表面維持外交承認的同時，暗中允許中共部隊在東北發展，並接收了龐大的日本關東軍軍事裝備與工業基礎。這使得原本以游擊戰為主的中共軍隊迅速現代化，演變成擁有重武器與鐵路後勤、足以進行大規模決戰的「東北野戰軍」，直接改變了雙方的實力起跑線。

美援的真實迷思與武器禁運

作者針對外界「美援龐大卻遭浪費」的迷思進行澄清。帳面上美國提供了超過16億美元的租借法案物資，但其中極大比例被計為運輸與後勤服務成本，前線部隊實際拿到的軍火裝備遠低於此數額。更為致命的是，在1946年至1947年內戰最為關鍵的轉折時刻，美國因政治考量對國民政府實施了武器禁運政策。對於高度依賴美式裝備與彈藥補給的國軍而言，後勤補給的無預警中斷成為極其沉重的毀滅性打擊，徹底重挫了國民政府的軍事優勢。

================================================

Many people surely have strong feelings about this question; some believe the KMT was ruined by the United States, while another group would say: >> Don't blame the US. The US gave the KMT so much aid; it was the KMT's own failure. First of all, the US certainly did provide aid to the Nationalist government. During the War of Resistance, the US helped train and equip the National Revolutionary Army, and after the war, it helped transport the troops to the Northeast and North China to take over occupied territories . US statistics show that the total Lend-Lease aid to the Republic of China exceeded $ 1.6 billion. However, this figure is easily misunderstood—it. wasn't $ 1.6 billion in cash, nor was it $ 1.6 billion worth of shells handed to the troops; a significant portion was actually for transport and services , which were listed as aid on the books . Therefore, the value of the weapons, ammunition, and equipment that actually reached the hands of the Nationalist troops was far lower than the $ 1.6 billion stated on paper. However, during the critical years of 1946 to 1947, the US implemented an arms embargo on the Nationalist army due to political issues. For a force highly dependent on American equipment, this. policy of cutting off supplies was a devastating blow. People often ask about the map in the background. This map is not just my dream map of the Republic of China's borders; it is what the Republic of China should look like in the hearts of 1.4 billion Chinese people. We aim to restore the Republic of China, using the Three Principles of the People from the National Revolution to carry out the mission of reclaiming the Republic and rebuilding the nation. We have launched a merchandise bundle featuring a map poster, a map tapestry, a map pillow, and a Republic of China flag keychain. Why choose when you can have it all? Take them all home for just 1911, and now, if you spend over 699 on either platform, you get free shipping. Friends overseas, don't worry. , we will launch international purchasing options soon. Hurry up and grab yours! >> Hello everyone, I'm A-Niu. Today we are going to talk about a question many people learned in history class but find truly incredible when they think about it carefully: Why did the KMT lose mainland China? Chiang Kai-shek in 1945 could be said to have had an incredible start, standing at the very peak of his life. As the leader of a founding member of the UN, commanding millions of American-equipped troops with international legal recognition, his regime seemed impregnable. Yet, in. just four short years, Nanjing, Shanghai, and Guangzhou fell one after another. How did this incredibly lopsided collapse in modern history happen? The central government had millions of regular troops, an air force, a navy, American equipment, and controlled China's most important cities, railways, and administrative bodies, all with US backing. On the other side, the Chinese Communist Party had only just come out of Yan'an, their main bases were in rural areas, and they were no match for the central government in terms of heavy weapons,. air power, or naval strength. Yet, just four years later, in 1949, Nanjing fell , Shanghai fell, Guangzhou fell, the entire mainland collapsed one after another, and the central government finally retreated to Taiwan. It is strange because the central government in 1945 held clear advantages in military, diplomatic, and international standing, yet the reversal over those four years is often oversimplified to " whoever wins the people, wins the world ." But if we examine the internal and external situation at the time, this saying fails to explain why the. Kuomintang held a winning hand only to lose it all so completely. The more you study this period of history, the more you realize that such an answer is far too simplistic. The central government certainly had serious problems: corruption, hyperinflation, low troop morale, land reform, and administrative inefficiency—each one worthy of critical review. So, if we reduce the entire Chinese Civil War to the Chinese Communist Party's main narrative that " the Chinese people chose the Communists ," we are being led by the nose, because many people overlook a massive.

factor when discussing why the KMT lost the war. The Chinese Civil War was never a fair match held behind closed doors between two Chinese parties; it occurred at a time when World War II had just ended and the US and the USSR were beginning a new struggle for the world order. In other words, the Civil War was not just a domestic conflict; it was also a part of the early international landscape of the Cold War . If we don't talk about the US, the Soviet Union, and Manchuria, we probably won't be able to truly understand how the Kuomintang ended up. losing. First, we must realize that although the central government in 1945 was ostensibly a victor, it was not a powerful state with a full treasury and abundant energy. The government was exactly the opposite. Since the start of the full-scale War of Resistance in 1937, the Republic of China had been fighting for eight consecutive years. Major cities like Shanghai, Nanjing, Wuhan, and Guangzhou had fallen one after another, and the most vital coastal industrial and commercial hubs, as well as tax revenue sources, had largely fallen under Japanese control. The fiscal foundation of the central government had already been uprooted. when it retreated to Chongqing. Facing bottomless war expenses, the only remaining option was to recklessly print money. The hyperinflation that erupted in 1946 was, in essence, a post-dated check issued during this long war of attrition. The severe postwar inflation did not suddenly appear in 1946; it was a massive lingering side effect of the eight-year war. The same was true militarily. Although the National Revolutionary Army boasted millions of men, its most elite units had been clashing head-on. with Japan’s best forces since the Battle of Shanghai. After eight years of war, the Republic of China had won the conflict, but it had paid a staggering price in fiscal and military strength. Therefore, while the central government appeared to be at the pinnacle of victory in 1945, the nation's foundation was, in reality, extremely weak. The biggest problem was that there was simply no time to rest and recuperate. Shortly after Japan surrendered, another, much larger war began, and the truly critical battlefield for this war was not in. Nanjing or Shanghai, but in the Northeast. It is hard for people today to imagine, but at the time, the Northeast was one of the most industrialized regions in all of China. During their occupation of Manchuria, the Japanese built massive railway, coal mining, steel, machinery, and military industries there. After the Japanese Kwantung Army surrendered, they left behind not just territory, but vast quantities of weapons, ammunition, military equipment, railways, and industrial foundations. Therefore, the Northeast in 1945 was less a piece of ordinary territory and more of a massive, super-sized arsenal. capable of changing the balance of military power between the Nationalists and the Communists. The question is, who was in the Northeast when Japan surrendered? Not the central government , but the Soviet Red Army. In August 1945, the Soviet Union declared war on Japan and quickly entered Northeast China, defeating the Kwantung Army. This created a very unique situation: while legally the Northeast should have been returned to the Republic of China, and internationally the Chinese central government was the Nationalist government, in reality, the major cities, transport lines, and Japanese. military supplies were under the actual control of the Soviet Army, which gave the CCP a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity. Some might say the Communist Party was entirely propped up by the Soviet Union, but that is too simplistic, because in 1945, Stalin did not initially openly bet on Mao Zedong. Diplomatically, the Soviet Union still formally recognized the Republic of China government and even signed the Treaty of Friendship and Alliance with it. However, as the situation developed , the Soviet Union did provide the CCP with very important conditions,.

including allowing the CCP to operate in parts of the Soviet-controlled areas , acquiring a portion of the Japanese-leftover weapons, and giving the CCP the vital time and space to enter the Northeast and establish bases . The impact of this was immense. During the war of resistance, the Communist army was primarily a guerrilla force lacking heavy weapons. But after reaching the Northeast, the Japanese weapons and ammunition, combined with the Northeast’s own industrial and railway systems, gave the CCP the conditions to gradually transform their original guerrilla. units into a regular army capable of large-scale combat against the Nationalist forces. The Soviet Union did not win the civil war for the CCP; rather, they directly changed the starting line for both sides. What was left behind in the Northeast was not just a few crates of rifles, but a complete war system including heavy weapons, railway networks, and a modern industrial base, which ultimately formed the Northeast Field Army capable of engaging the Nationalist forces in major decisive battles. But even more interesting is what was happening on the other side. While the Soviet Union. was creating this strategic environment in the Northeast, what was the Republic of China’s most important ally, the United States, doing? This is a question many people will surely argue about; some believe that >> the Nationalist Party was doomed by the United States, >> while another group will say >> Forget the US; the US gave the KMT so much aid, the KMT was just too incompetent itself. Actually, both sides are only half right. First of all , of course the US provided aid to the Nationalist government. During the War of Resistance, the US helped train and equip the Nationalist army, and after the war, it helped transport them to. the Northeast and North China to receive surrendered territories. The US recorded total Lend-Lease aid to the Republic of China at over 1.6 billion dollars, but this figure easily causes misunderstandings; it was not 1.6 billion in cash, nor did it all go toward artillery shells for the Nationalist army. A significant portion actually consisted of transportation and services, such as helping to move Nationalist troops to North China and the Northeast, which are included in the aid balance sheet, so the actual value of weapons, ammunition, and equipment directly in the hands of the. army was far lower than the 1.6 billion dollar figure. Furthermore, compared to US investment in other major allies, the aid received by the Republic of China was surprisingly low; the Soviet Union received several times more, to say nothing of the scale provided to Britain. Therefore, the claim that "the US armed the KMT to the teeth, only for them to hand all their gear to the Communists" tends to overestimate the actual scale of the aid and the portion that could be directly used in the Chinese Civil War. But that is not the. most important issue; the most important thing is that US aid to the Nationalist government did not mean the US was willing to help destroy the Communists. With World War II just over , the last thing the US wanted to see was an immediate, large-scale civil war in China involving millions. It was a total civil war, which is why Truman sent Marshall to China to mediate. The US hoped for a ceasefire, negotiations, and KMT-CCP cooperation, but Chiang Kai-shek believed the CCP was expanding rapidly and would only be harder to deal with later, so the Republic of. China and the US fundamentally lacked shared strategic goals on whether to fight this war to the end. This leads to a highly controversial issue, often rumored as "the US provided guns but no bullets," but the truth lies in a more complex logistical breakdown. The Nationalist army began re-equipping with US gear at the end of the war, but during the critical years of 1946 to 1947, the US imposed an arms embargo on the Nationalist army due to political issues; for a force highly dependent on.

American equipment, this policy was a lethal blow. Even US government documents acknowledged that the deterioration of the Nationalist army's situation at the time, besides issues with high-level command and morale, was also significantly hampered by a shortage of ammunition. So a more accurate statement is that it wasn't that the US never provided bullets, but rather that after the Nationalist army partially Americanized, it faced political restrictions on arms procurement from the US at a crucial stage of the civil war, and this impact cannot be ignored. But we cannot blame. America entirely, as the Nationalist Army's own ammunition management and logistics systems had serious flaws. Caught in the cracks on the eve of the US-Soviet Cold War, the central government faced a very awkward diplomatic situation. America, ostensibly an ally, had a strategic bottom line of avoiding entanglement in a full-scale Asian war and thus worked hard to contain the civil war, while the Soviet Union, which recognized the Republic of China by treaty, secretly ceded space and supplies in the Northeast to bolster the CCP. When the. strategic goals of an ally diverge from one's own survival interests, foreign aid can actually become a political shackle, which is why the central government faced such a difficult international environment. America was not an enemy, but rather our most important ally; however, the outcome the U.S. desired was not the outcome Chiang Kai-shek wanted. This is why I do not believe 1949 can be explained solely by the Nationalist Party losing popular support. The CCP’s primary narrative regarding the Civil War is that "the Nationalist Party lost the. people's hearts, so the Communists won the world." In an era without universal suffrage, military victory and democratic mandate cannot be equated. What the CCP demonstrated was not democratic consensus based on votes, but precise interest-based exchanges and organizational mobilization. For impoverished tenant farmers, the abstract "Five-Power Constitution" could not compare to the immediate prospect of land redistribution. The Communist Party's organizational ability in rural areas was indeed far superior to the Nationalists. Rent reduction, land reform, peasant associations, militias, party branches,. and political propaganda—the CCP wove all these elements together. For many poor farmers, land was the most direct benefit. If you go to someone today who has no fields and cannot get enough to eat...If you talk to a starving farmer about freedom, democracy, or the constitution, he might not understand; but if the Communist Party tells him, " Follow me, and the landlord's land will be given to you," he certainly understands that. Of course, the CCP's subsequent land reform was accompanied by cruel class struggle, violence, and killing. We cannot romanticize it, but from the perspective of war. mobilization alone, it was highly effective. The CCP integrated peasants, food, intelligence, recruitment, and transport entirely into their party structure. So the situation was more like the Nationalists had the state, while the Communists had better organization. However, having the ability to mobilize the masses does not equate to receiving a democratic mandate from all Chinese people. Therefore, a more accurate statement is that the Nationalists lost the world, not that the Communists won the people's hearts. The outcome of war is inherently the result of a combination. of military, organizational, financial, diplomatic, and international factors. If we blame the Nationalist failure entirely on the U.S. and the Soviet Union, we are simply moving from one form of historical reductionism to another. The Nationalist government faced its own severe problems, the first and most fatal being hyperinflation. The Nationalist government had been printing money in massive quantities since the War of Resistance, and the astronomical military spending after the civil war broke out caused the fiscal situation to collapse. In 1947 alone, the.

issuance of legal tender increased more than eightfold, while rice prices in Shanghai surged over 15 times, with the majority of government spending diverted to the military. By 1948, the situation was completely out of control . The Nationalist government introduced the Gold Yuan, hoping to solve the inflation issue in one stroke, and even demanded that the people exchange their gold, silver, and foreign currency for these notes. Soon after its launch, the Gold Yuan plummeted in value, leading to dire consequences because who relied on currency the most? Civil servants, teachers, soldiers, the middle class,. and business owners in the cities. Farmers at least had land and food, but for a professor in Shanghai or a civil servant in Nanjing, their salaries would become worthless scraps of paper within days of receipt. How could they not lose faith in the government? So it seemed that before the Communists even entered Shanghai, the Nationalist government had already destroyed its own urban base through hyperinflation. The second issue was government credibility, but it must be clarified that in 1945, at the time of victory in the war, the central government was not. without prestige. On the contrary, Chiang Kai-shek and the Nationalist government were at the peak of their popularity. After eight years of war, the Republic of China had finally become a victor. Many people in the occupied territories truly longed for the central government to return, and the Nationalist troops were welcomed by crowds when they entered cities like Shanghai and Nanjing. Therefore, the problem in 1945 was not that the people didn't trust the Nationalist government , but rather that their expectations for it were too high. Everyone thought that with the war finally over, what. would follow was peaceful reconstruction, economic recovery, and constitutional development; however, the reality of the ensuing years was a massive disappointment. The post-war takeover was marred by widespread chaos and corruption, even being mocked by the public as "taking over the spoils." As the fighting expanded, from the conscription of troops and grain to the total collapse of fiscal policy, the public's optimistic expectations for the new regime rapidly turned into a severe collapse of confidence within just two or three years. The political credibility of the Nationalist. government did not vanish suddenly in 1945; instead, it was rapidly depleted from a very high position between 1946 and 1948. By the later stages of the Chinese Civil War, what the central government had truly lost was less about abstract prestige and more about the shift from the public's high expectations in 1945 to their deep disappointment in the government's ability to govern. The third issue is the military; many people would say the Nationalist army was just too incompetent and was crushed by the Communist forces. But this explanation is far too simplistic. The Nationalist army was not entirely incapable of. fighting; the War of Resistance and the Burma Campaign both proved that certain Nationalist units possessed significant combat effectiveness. The real problem was that the Nationalist army was never a highly integrated and assimilated modern national force. It consisted of central troops, local provincial forces , former warlord units, absorbed troops , and even reorganized puppet forces after the war, with massive disparities in loyalty, training, equipment, and combat morale among them. Furthermore, Chiang Kai-shek’s high level of intervention in military command and his lack of trust in his generals,. combined with internal factionalism, created issues. Once the economy began to collapse, military purchasing power plummeted, logistics failed, and with a large influx of forced conscripts, the entire force began to lose its resilience. Therefore, the Kuomintang’s loss of the mainland cannot be attributed solely to Chiang Kai-shek’s inability to lead troops in battle. As the supreme leader, Chiang naturally bears the ultimate political responsibility for the failure, but the total collapse of an army of millions and a nation of hundreds of millions within a few years.

could not have been caused by one person’s military ability alone. By 1948, all the problems the Kuomintang had accumulated began to explode at once, starting with the Liaoshen Campaign, which is why we spent so much time discussing the Northeast earlier. Once the Northeast was lost, the central government didn’t just lose a vast territory and a large number of elite frontline troops; more importantly, the CCP gained real control over major industrial hubs and military bases. Next was the Xuzhou-Bengbu Campaign, which even more clearly highlighted the gap in. organizational capabilities between the Kuomintang and the Communists. The CCP was able to mobilize a massive number of peasants to assist in transporting food, ammunition, and the wounded. This doesn’t mean every peasant pushing a cart was a devout communist; it truly demonstrates that the Party’s organization had penetrated the grassroots, turning the vast resources of a rural society into war-fighting capability. After the Pingjin Campaign ended and the situation in North China was settled, the Kuomintang suffered a total collapse at this point. My view. is that it wasn't the loss of the three major campaigns that caused the sudden loss of China; rather, the Nationalist government’s finances, political credibility, military morale, grassroots organization, and international standing had all faced severe problems simultaneously, and the three campaigns simply brought all these issues to a head. We can finally answer today's question: why did the Kuomintang lose the entire mainland? It was not due to a single reason, nor can it be explained by the simple phrase of "losing the hearts and minds of the. people." On the surface, the Kuomintang possessed everything a modern state should have: a central government, an army, diplomatic recognition, a central bank, administrative agencies, and international allies. However, a truly effective modern state requires more than just flying a flag or setting up ministries. You must be able to stabilize the currency, collect taxes, govern regions, maintain effective logistics, nationalize the military, promote social reform, gain the people's trust, and at the same time, secure a favorable strategic environment in international politics. By 1948-49, the central government was steadily losing these capabilities, which is why I would argue that what the Kuomintang truly lost was its state capacity. The Nationalist government's own governance crisis, combined with the CCP's stronger grassroots organizational ability and the post-WWII shift in U.S. policy toward China, together determined the outcome of the civil war. However, this leads to a very interesting question: if the KMT truly lacked any governance ability , had completely lost popular support, and was destined to be discarded by. history, why didn't it lose again after retreating to Taiwan, but instead managed to slowly stabilize? I believe this is exactly the most thought-provoking aspect of analyzing this history. After the central government withdrew to Taiwan, it accomplished many things it had failed or lacked the capacity to do on the mainland: restructuring finances, stabilizing the currency, reorganizing the military, improving the administrative system, and most importantly, land reform—starting with the 375 Rent Reduction in 1949, followed by the sale of public land, and leading to the "Land to the Tiller" program in 1953, which turned many. tenant farmers into landowners. Has everyone noticed a rather ironic fact? The land issue was never the exclusive domain of the Communist Party. The Founding Father, Sun Yat-sen, had already proposed the "equalization of land rights" in the Three Principles of the People; the National Revolution understood from the beginning that if a country's land and wealth are highly concentrated and the vast majority of farmers lack basic economic security, it is very difficult to achieve true political and social stability. The problem was that while on the mainland, the central government was constrained by wars, warlords, local factions, and.

the existing social structure, making it impossible to fully implement the equalization of land rights. The Communist Party, instead, used more radical—even violent and class-struggle-driven—methods to seize this key political issue that originally belonged to the Three Principles of the People. After reaching Taiwan, the KMT finally had the opportunity, within a smaller territory where government control was more intact, to truly carry out land reform. Therefore, I believe the fact that the KMT was able to gain a firm footing in Taiwan proves that its failure on the mainland did not. represent a failure of the Three Principles of the People itself; rather , it was because the central government of that time simply did not have enough time to complete the National Revolution. Thus, 1949 cannot be simply described as the Chinese people abandoning the KMT for the CCP, because the Chinese people never made such a choice in a free election. What truly happened in 1949 was that the Republic of China, having just endured eight years of war, with a near-collapsed economy and an exhausted society, was immediately plunged into another full-scale civil war. It faced a CCP. that had secured strategic conditions in Manchuria and possessed immense grassroots organizational power, while simultaneously dealing with a United States that preferred mediation and was unwilling to support the destruction of the CCP, as well as a Soviet Union that nominally recognized the Republic of China but provided the CCP with critical conditions for growth—all this, combined with the government's own hyperinflation, corruption, insufficient land reform, and issues with its military and administrative systems, resulted in the events of 1949 . Therefore, I believe the collapse of the KMT in 1949 was not simply a military defeat on paper, but the. result of the state's fiscal, organizational, diplomatic, and military systems unraveling after eight years of war, before a modern national framework had even been established. But in the end, I want to return to what this channel has always cared about most: the KMT losing the mainland in 1949 does not mean the National Revolution failed, because its goal was never to keep the KMT in power forever. Regrettably, by 1949, these goals had not yet been fully achieved. While the CCP won the civil war militarily, they did not complete China's democratic revolution; instead, they established a. totalitarian regime under one-party rule. So, our discussion today on why the KMT lost mainland China is not meant to vindicate them. Our true purpose is to look back at this massive historical failure to better understand what a truly modernized China actually requires. What it needs is not an infallible great leader, but democratic constitutionalism, a nationalized military, an effective and accountable government, localized governance, and a. system for the people to share in the fruits of development—all of which the National Revolution began seeking over a century ago. It is just that this path has been incredibly long and filled with failures, to the point where we nearly lost all of China in 1949. The Republic of China’s eventual transition to democracy in Taiwan proves that Chinese people are not incapable of democracy, nor are they destined to accept one-party rule.
